scope: These are educational mappings of controls to principles, not compliance certifications. Legal duties depend on jurisdiction, system classification, your role, and applicable dates. OECD principles and NIST guidance are not legislation.

statuses.present: Implemented and backed by evidence in the codebase.
statuses.partial: Some of the control exists, but part of the action or its enforcement is missing.
statuses.not_applicable: Does not apply to this agent (a reason is required).
statuses.unknown: Cannot be decided from the code alone; needs an answer from the team.

traits.label: Takes actions
traits.question: Does the agent write, send or change anything outside its own run?
traits.trueWhen: It writes to a database, file or queue, calls an API that changes something, or sends a message. Calling a model API on its own doesn't count.
traits.whenFalse: it only returns text and changes nothing outside its own run

traits.label: Consequential actions
traits.question: Can any action be hard to undo, or affect people outside the team?
traits.trueWhen: It moves money, deletes or overwrites records other people rely on, contacts people outside the system, changes access or permissions, runs generated code, or publishes something.
traits.whenFalse: none of its actions is hard to undo or affects people outside the team

traits.label: Consequential actions without review
traits.question: Does any consequential action take effect before a person approves that specific action?
traits.trueWhen: The agent executes the action itself. False only when every consequential output lands as a draft or proposal that a person approves before it takes effect.
traits.whenFalse: every consequential output is a draft that a person approves before it takes effect

traits.label: Model makes decisions
traits.question: Does model output choose a target, amount, category, priority or route that is acted on or recorded?
traits.trueWhen: A model's answer decides what happens next or what gets stored, beyond being shown to a person as free text.
traits.whenFalse: model output is only shown to a person and never decides an action or a stored value

traits.label: Resolves ambiguous targets
traits.question: Does the agent work out who or what to act on from free text or fuzzy matching?
traits.trueWhen: It turns names, descriptions or phrases like "my last order" into a specific customer, record, recipient or file.
traits.whenFalse: every target it acts on arrives as an explicit identifier

accountability.name: Accountability
accountability.question: Who is responsible?
accountability.definition: Assign responsibility and keep evidence so people can answer for the system’s actions.

transparency.name: Transparency
transparency.question: What should people know?
transparency.definition: Make the use of AI, its capabilities, and its limitations clear to the people using or affected by it.

explainability.name: Explainability
explainability.question: Why this outcome?
explainability.definition: Give people understandable, faithful reasons for a particular outcome, grounded in the evidence that actually mattered.

oversight.name: Human oversight
oversight.question: Can a person intervene?
oversight.definition: Give informed people the authority and practical means to question, refuse, override, or stop the system.

reliability.name: Reliability & robustness
reliability.question: Does it work under stress?
reliability.definition: Test performance for the intended use, including failures and changing conditions, and keep that evidence current.

safety.name: Safety & security
safety.question: Can harm be contained?
safety.definition: Reduce foreseeable harm and misuse, constrain dangerous capabilities, and recover or stop safely.

privacy.name: Privacy & data governance
privacy.question: Is personal data protected?
privacy.definition: Limit data collection and access, define retention, and protect people’s information throughout its use.

fairness.name: Fairness & contestability
fairness.question: Is treatment fair and challengeable?
fairness.definition: Assess harmful bias and unequal impacts, and provide a meaningful way to challenge outcomes and obtain review.

oecdAccountability.title: OECD · Principle 1.5
oecdAccountability.detail: Responsibility, traceability, and ongoing risk management across the AI lifecycle.

oecdTransparency.title: OECD · Principle 1.3
oecdTransparency.detail: Meaningful disclosure of capabilities, limitations, and reasons for outcomes, enabling people to challenge them.

oecdSafety.title: OECD · Principle 1.4
oecdSafety.detail: Robust, secure operation and the ability to override, repair, or safely retire harmful systems.

oecdRights.title: OECD · Principle 1.2
oecdRights.detail: Human rights, fairness, privacy, and human agency throughout the lifecycle.

nist.title: NIST · AI RMF 1.0, §3
nist.detail: Trustworthiness includes reliability, safety, security, accountability, transparency, explainability, privacy, and managed harmful bias. Version 1.0 (2023); revision in progress.

eu12.title: EU AI Act · Article 12
eu12.detail: Automatic event logging to support traceability, monitoring, and risk identification for high-risk AI systems.

eu13.title: EU AI Act · Article 13
eu13.detail: Information that lets deployers interpret outputs, understand limitations, and use high-risk AI appropriately.

eu14.title: EU AI Act · Article 14
eu14.detail: Effective human oversight, including appropriate intervention, override, and interruption into a safe state.

eu15.title: EU AI Act · Article 15
eu15.detail: Appropriate accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity throughout a high-risk system’s lifecycle.

eu86.title: EU AI Act · Article 86
eu86.detail: An explanation right for certain adversely affecting, legally or similarly significant decisions based on Annex III high-risk AI, subject to the article’s exclusions and conditions.

widerGovernance.note: These rooms provide some access and record controls. They still need a data inventory, minimisation, lawful processing where required, retention rules, and privacy assessment.
Reliability tests and audit records can support review. They still need group-specific evaluation, bias mitigation, accessible challenge routes, and meaningful remedies.

rooms.title: The Passport Checkpoint
rooms.question: Can every action be attributed?
rooms.summary: Every outgoing action carries a signed chain connecting its accountable owner, agent build, running instance, and individual session.
risks: Plain identity headers can be forged
Reused instance IDs mix separate processes

limitation.title: A valid identity can still perform a harmful action.
limitation.body: The passport proves which credential acted, not whether the action was permitted or correct. A compromised credential can produce correctly signed requests; even complete attribution cannot prevent harm on its own.

companions.reason: Limit what the identified caller can do, even when its signature is valid.
Preserve the verified identity with intent and outcome so an incident can be reconstructed.
Revoke the compromised instance’s authority and block further work.

governance.headline: An action has an accountable owner.

mappings.contribution: The signed passport connects each action to an owner, agent, instance, and session. An investigator can follow responsibility back to its source.
mappings.evidence: Verified identity claims linked to action records.

mappings.contribution: Attribution supplies the “who acted?” part of a useful explanation and helps identify the responsible operator.
mappings.evidence: A traceable owner and a documented contact for review.

governance.remaining: Signed identifiers do not explain a decision or establish legal accountability on their own. Define real responsibilities, disclose AI use, and give people a route to human review.

checks.title: Define the identity contract
checks.action: Write down, in one fixed format, the four things every agent must declare about itself: the person or team accountable for it, which version of the agent it is, which running copy it is, and which task it is working on. Give every agent you switch on a named owner.
checks.verify: Try to start an agent that is missing its owner or its version. It should refuse to start and say plainly what was missing.
lookFor: A declared owner/team and agent build or version for each deployed agent (config, manifest, deployment metadata, env schema).
Startup validation that refuses to run when owner or build identity is missing.
notEnough: An owner named only in a README or CODEOWNERS with nothing read at runtime.
checks.fix: Add a typed identity config (owner, agent name, build/version) loaded at startup and fail fast when any field is missing.

checks.title: Separate process and session lifetimes
checks.action: Give each running copy of the agent a brand-new ID every time it starts, and carry the task's own ID unchanged through every tool it uses, every retry, and every background job.
checks.verify: Restart the agent and run two tasks at once. The running-copy ID should change after the restart, and the two tasks should stay clearly separate even when work happens in the background.
lookFor: A fresh instance ID generated per process start (uuid at boot), distinct from the session/thread/conversation ID.
The session ID propagated through tool calls, retries, and background/queued work.
notEnough: A single hard-coded agent name used as the only identifier.
checks.fix: Generate an instance ID at process start, keep the framework's session/thread ID, and pass both in a context object to every tool and queued job.

checks.title: Issue claims outside the agent’s trust boundary
checks.action: Have a separate, trusted service hand out each agent's proof of identity. Keep the secret keys that sign that proof somewhere the AI itself can never reach, and make sure the agent cannot claim to be a different owner.
checks.verify: Try to get an identity pass made out to someone else, and try to use one the agent signed for itself. Both attempts should be refused — either by the service that issues passes or by the service receiving the request.
lookFor: Credentials obtained from a workload/managed identity, OIDC, or token service rather than static secrets.
Signing keys and identity selection kept out of tools the model can call.
notEnough: A long-lived shared API key in env/config used by several agents.
The agent choosing its own owner/principal from model output or request input.
checks.fix: Replace shared static keys with a per-agent workload identity (cloud managed identity, OIDC client credentials, SPIFFE) and keep issuance outside the agent process.

checks.title: Verify claims at every receiving boundary
checks.action: Before any service acts on a request, it should check the identity pass: that the signature is genuine, that it came from the trusted issuer, that it was meant for this service, that it has not expired, and that all the required details are present.
checks.verify: Send passes that are tampered with, expired, meant for a different service, or missing details. Every service should reject them before anything actually happens.
lookFor: Receiving services/tools/MCP servers validate token signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and required claims before acting.
notEnough: Trusting a plain header such as `X-Agent-Name` or a field in the request body.
Verifying signature but not audience/expiry.
checks.fix: Validate a signed token at each tool/API boundary (signature + iss + aud + exp + required identity claims) and reject before any side effect.

checks.title: Bound token lifetime and revocation delay
checks.action: Decide how long an identity pass stays valid and how quickly you can cancel one. Write down how you replace the signing keys and how you switch off an agent that is already running.
checks.verify: Replace a signing key and switch off a test agent. Check that its old access stops working within the time limit you committed to.
lookFor: Short token lifetimes, key rotation config, and a way to disable a single agent instance or principal.
notEnough: Tokens or keys with no expiry; rotation described only in prose.
checks.fix: Set an explicit maximum token lifetime, document rotation, and add a per-instance disable/deny list checked at the boundary.

checks.title: Route all external calls through enforcement
checks.action: List every way the agent can reach the outside world — web requests, code libraries, background queues, built-in tools. Make each destination require a verified identity, and block any route that would let the agent skip that check.
checks.verify: Try to make the agent act on the outside world through a back door — a direct connection or a direct code call. Neither should be able to skip the identity check.
lookFor: All outbound HTTP/SDK/queue calls go through one wrapped client that attaches identity.
Lint rules, scanners, or code review rules that forbid raw clients in agent code.
notEnough: A wrapper exists but tools also call `requests`/`httpx`/`fetch`/SDKs directly.
checks.fix: Route every tool's external call through one identity-attaching client and add a lint/scan rule that fails CI on raw client imports in agent modules.

checks.title: Carry verified identity into the ledger
checks.action: On every record — the plan, the steps taken, and the result — attach the identity that the receiving service actually confirmed, plus one shared ID that ties those records together. Do not write the pass itself into the records.
checks.verify: Follow one background action from start to finish. Every record along the way should point to the same owner, version, running copy, task, and action — and none should expose the secret pass.
lookFor: Logs/traces/audit records carry owner, build, instance, session, and a shared action ID.
Bearer tokens are not written to logs.
notEnough: Logs with timestamps and messages but no attributable identity or correlation ID.
checks.fix: Attach verified identity fields and an action ID to the trace context and every ledger record; scrub Authorization headers from logs.

checks.title: Exercise a compromised-credential scenario
checks.action: In a safe test environment, take a genuine test identity and use it to attempt something it is not allowed to do, then switch that agent off using the Shutdown controls.
checks.verify: The Permission safeguard should block the action, the Ledger should keep a record that it was blocked, and once the cut-off time passes, any further attempts by that agent should fail.
lookFor: A test or runbook that uses a valid identity for an unauthorized action and then revokes it.
notEnough: Unit tests that only cover the happy path for authentication.
checks.fix: Add a staging test: valid test identity + forbidden action must be denied and recorded, and calls must fail after revoking that instance.

rooms.title: The Proof Bridge
rooms.question: Has every part proved reliable?
rooms.summary: Every retrieval, transformation, reasoning step, and tool contract earns its own fresh reliability certificate before joining the workflow.
risks: Small failure rates compound across long chains
End-to-end demos hide the weakest link

limitation.title: Passing parts can still form a failing system.
limitation.body: Tests sample known conditions. Interfaces, production drift, and unfamiliar inputs can defeat a workflow whose components all passed. A certificate is evidence for a tested version and context, not a guarantee of future correctness.

companions.reason: Hold decisions when required evidence is missing or outside the validated operating range.
Capture production failures and their versions so evaluation suites can learn from them.
Contain a live failure when monitoring crosses a defined error or impact limit.

governance.headline: Trust rests on current test evidence.

mappings.contribution: Every span earns fresh evidence before the workflow crosses. Testing parts and interfaces exposes weaknesses that a successful demo can hide.
mappings.evidence: Version-bound evaluations, interface tests, and end-to-end results.

mappings.contribution: A failed span blocks release, keeping a known defect from becoming a consequential action.
mappings.evidence: Failure cases, release thresholds, and a blocked-release record.

mappings.contribution: The certificate records what was tested and which version passed, so a release decision can be examined later.
mappings.evidence: Test ownership and a recorded release decision.

governance.remaining: Passing tests is not a guarantee of safe or fair operation. Evaluate real-world conditions, affected groups, system interactions, and performance after deployment.

checks.title: Map the workflow and its contracts
checks.action: List every step in the agent's work — each time it looks something up, reshapes information, makes a judgement, or uses a tool. For each one, note who owns it, what goes in and what comes out, what it depends on, and what should happen if it fails.
checks.verify: Follow one typical request through your map. Every step, and every hand-off between steps, should have an owner and a clear description of what it expects and what it produces.
lookFor: Typed input/output schemas between steps (Pydantic/dataclasses/TypedDict/Zod/JSON Schema), including tool schemas.
A documented or code-defined workflow graph with owners and failure policy.
notEnough: Free-form dicts/strings passed between steps with no schema.
checks.fix: Give every retrieval, model, and tool step a typed input/output contract and document the step graph with an owner and failure policy per step.

checks.title: Create isolated tests for each stage
checks.action: Sort each step into one of three kinds: steps that always give the same answer, steps that talk to other systems, and steps that rely on the AI's judgement. For each, build a repeatable set of tests covering both the expected results and the common ways it goes wrong.
checks.verify: Run each step's tests on their own in your automated test run, and deliberately plant a fault in one step. That step's own tests should catch it — you should not need the full start-to-finish run to notice.
lookFor: Separate tests per stage (retrieval, tool, transformation, model step) that run in isolation, with mocks for neighbours.
notEnough: Only an end-to-end smoke test or a notebook demo.
checks.fix: Create one test module per workflow stage with its own expected outcomes and failure cases, and run them in CI.

checks.title: Gate deterministic code on required invariants
checks.action: For the predictable, rule-based parts of the code, test that they handle the expected format, the edge values, the calculations, and the moves from one state to the next. If any must-pass check fails, do not release.
checks.verify: Run the edge-case and rule checks. Every required one must pass, and write down exactly what you tested rather than claiming it is correct in every possible case.
lookFor: Boundary, arithmetic, schema, and state-transition tests for deterministic code (e.g. refund amounts, date windows); property-based tests where useful.
notEnough: Tests that only assert the function returns without error.
checks.fix: Add boundary and property tests for money, dates, limits, and state transitions, and block release on failure.

checks.title: Inject dependency failures
checks.action: Test what happens when the systems the agent relies on misbehave: garbled data, no reply in time, being told to slow down, the same answer arriving twice, or a job that only half-finishes. Decide how many times to retry, and make sure an action that runs twice does not cause its effect twice.
checks.verify: Simulate the agent saving something and then timing out before it hears back, so it cannot tell whether the save worked. On recovery it should either confirm what actually happened or safely retry — without doing the same thing twice.
lookFor: Tests that inject timeouts, malformed payloads, rate limits, duplicates, and partial failures.
Bounded retries with idempotency keys for side-effecting calls.
notEnough: Unbounded or blind retries around writes; `except Exception: pass`.
checks.fix: Bound retries, add idempotency keys to side-effecting calls, and test timeout-after-write recovery.

checks.title: Set measurable model acceptance criteria
checks.action: Decide, for your particular use, how many mistakes are acceptable. Test against realistic samples of the different kinds of case you will actually see, use enough examples to trust the result, and note how much the measurement itself could be off.
checks.verify: Test on examples the model has not seen before, including the mistakes that would do the most damage. The results, and the margin of error around them, must meet the pass mark you set in advance.
lookFor: An evaluation dataset (golden set) with domain-specific metrics and pass thresholds (promptfoo, deepeval, ragas, inspect, LangSmith, Braintrust, vendor evals, or custom).
Consequential failure cases in the dataset, not just happy paths.
notEnough: Manual spot checks; eval scripts with no threshold that can fail.
checks.fix: Create an eval dataset with consequential edge cases, define per-metric thresholds, and make the eval job fail when a threshold is missed.

checks.title: Bind release evidence to the deployed version
checks.action: Keep a record of exactly which versions you are shipping — the code, the AI model, the instructions it is given, the data, the settings, and the tests you ran. If any of these changes, the old test results no longer count for the parts affected.
checks.verify: Change an instruction or an underlying component after testing. The release check should then insist on fresh test results for the parts that changed before it lets you ship.
lookFor: Model, prompt, tool schema, and code versions pinned and recorded together with the eval results that justified the release.
notEnough: Floating model aliases (e.g. `latest`) and prompts edited inline with no version.
checks.fix: Pin model and prompt versions, record them in a release manifest with eval results, and re-run evals when any of them change.

checks.title: Test joins and complete journeys
checks.action: Test that the steps fit together correctly and that whole, realistic journeys work from start to finish — including permission checks, retries, cancelling midway, and one step passing bad information to the next. Run these automatically.
checks.verify: Make two steps stop fitting together while each step still passes its own separate tests. The combined-journey check should catch the mismatch and stop the release.
lookFor: Interface/contract tests between stages and representative end-to-end scenarios that run in CI and block merge/deploy.
notEnough: Integration tests that exist but are not part of any CI gate.
checks.fix: Add contract tests for each handoff and an end-to-end scenario suite as a required CI check.

checks.title: Rehearse failure after a passing release
checks.action: Once the agent is live, set up alerts for rising errors and for the system slowly drifting away from how it behaved in testing. Give each alert an owner and a deadline to respond, and connect them to either pausing the agent or stopping it under supervision.
checks.verify: In a test environment, feed in something well outside the normal range and a steady run of failures. Confirm the agent pauses or stops, that the Ledger keeps the evidence, and that someone is assigned to investigate.
lookFor: Production monitoring of error rates and quality (sampled evals, trace analytics) with alert thresholds and owners.
Alerts wired to a hold or a supervised stop (drift → shutdown).
notEnough: Dashboards with no alert thresholds or owners.
checks.fix: Define production error/drift alerts with owners and connect sustained breaches to the uncertainty hold or the stop path.

rooms.title: The Single-Use Vault
rooms.question: What is the agent allowed to do?
rooms.summary: Ordinary tools stay available. Consequential actions remain locked until a human grants a signed, exact, single-use approval.
risks: A hallucination becomes an irreversible action
Prompt injection reaches a dangerous tool
Broad approvals become reusable master keys

limitation.title: Approval fatigue can turn a strong lock into a formality.
limitation.body: Exact, single-use approval enforces a person’s decision, including a mistaken one. Excessive prompts, weak evidence, or time pressure can encourage rubber-stamping. The other rooms support review and containment; reviewer capacity still needs its own design.

companions.reason: Resolve missing facts before requesting approval, so the reviewer sees one well-specified action.
Record proposals and decisions; review approval volume and outcomes for signs that oversight is failing.
Stop further execution if an approved action starts causing harm; completed effects may still need remediation.

governance.headline: Human authority has an enforceable boundary.

mappings.contribution: A human can refuse the exact consequential action before it executes. The single-use key gives that decision a real technical boundary.
mappings.evidence: The exact request, approver, scope, expiry, and one-time use.

mappings.contribution: The vault limits what an injected or mistaken instruction can cause. A broad or reused approval cannot silently open more actions.
mappings.evidence: Denied requests and tests that reject altered or reused approvals.

mappings.contribution: The approval binds an identified person to a specific authorization rather than leaving a reusable blanket permission.
mappings.evidence: An attributable approval and execution record.

governance.remaining: An approval button is meaningful only if the reviewer has enough information, time, competence, and authority to refuse. This key design is an implementation choice, not a prescribed legal mechanism.

checks.title: Inventory and classify executable capabilities
checks.action: Make a table of every tool and action the agent can perform. For each, note how risky it is, where it is allowed to reach, who must approve it, and — for anything not on the list — set the default answer to no.
checks.verify: Add a new tool or destination that has not been classified yet. The agent should not be able to use it until someone has written down the rules for it.
lookFor: An explicit registry of tools/actions with risk level, allowed destinations, and required approval.
Deny-by-default for unknown tools or destinations.
notEnough: All tools registered equally with no risk classification.
checks.fix: Create a tool registry that classifies each tool (read / internal write / consequential), lists allowed destinations, and blocks anything unclassified.

checks.title: Enforce policy where the side effect occurs
checks.action: Enforce the rules at the point where the action actually takes effect — in the gateway the agent passes through, or in the service receiving the request. Remove any direct access keys and block any route out that would skip the gateway.
checks.verify: Try the same risky action three ways: through the normal tool, through a direct code call, and through a direct web request. All three should be stopped by the same rules.
lookFor: Authorization enforced inside the tool wrapper, gateway, or receiving service — where the side effect happens.
No direct credentials or raw SDK/HTTP paths that can perform the consequential action without the check.
notEnough: A system prompt telling the model to ask first.
A framework interrupt/confirm UI that the tool function itself does not depend on.
checks.fix: Move the approval check into the consequential tool's execution path (wrapper or receiving API) so the side effect cannot run without it, and remove bypass paths.

checks.title: Bind approval to the complete action
checks.action: Tie each approval to the exact action it is for: what is being done, to what, with which details, by which agent and task, under which request, and until when. Lock that down with a signature, and include the version of whatever is being changed so a later change breaks the match.
checks.verify: After something is approved, change one detail — the amount, the recipient, a setting, or the version of what is being changed. The agent should see it no longer matches the approval, refuse to proceed, and ask for a fresh approval.
lookFor: Approvals bound to the exact operation and arguments (canonical hash of tool + args), target, session, and expiry; mismatch is rejected.
notEnough: A boolean `approved=True` flag or a generic 'allow this tool' permission.
checks.fix: Issue approvals as signed tokens containing a hash of the canonical tool name + arguments + session + expiry, and verify the hash against the actual call.

checks.title: Build a review screen that supports refusal
checks.action: Give the approver a screen showing exactly what the agent wants to do, the evidence behind it, how confident it is, and what the consequences would be. Make sure that person is who they say they are and is allowed to decide, and give them an obvious way to say no.
checks.verify: Someone without permission should not be able to approve at all. Someone with permission should be able to review the request and reject it — and nothing should happen as a result of rejecting it.
lookFor: An approval UI/message showing the exact action, arguments, evidence, and consequences, with a clear deny, restricted to authorized reviewers.
notEnough: A generic 'Agent wants to use tool X — Allow?' prompt; any user able to approve.
checks.fix: Render the exact proposed action with its arguments, evidence, and impact, require an authorized reviewer role, and offer an explicit deny.

checks.title: Consume approvals atomically
checks.action: Keep track of approvals somewhere the agent cannot tamper with, make them expire quickly, and make sure each approval can only be spent once even if two attempts arrive at the same moment. Tag retries so a repeated attempt cannot act twice.
checks.verify: Use the same approval twice at once, then try to reuse it again after it has expired. At most one action should actually happen, and the expired one should fail.
lookFor: Approval state stored outside the agent (DB/cache) with short expiry, consumed atomically (compare-and-set / unique nonce / jti), plus an execution idempotency key.
notEnough: Approvals kept in process memory or reusable until restart.
checks.fix: Store approvals in a durable store, consume each nonce atomically before executing, enforce expiry, and pass an idempotency key to the side-effecting API.

checks.title: Design and measure the review workload
checks.action: Decide which serious actions truly need a person to approve them, who handles the approval queue, how much they can handle, and what happens when it is too much. Let low-risk work proceed within set limits instead of asking a person about everything.
checks.verify: Flood the approval queue with a realistic number of requests and reviewers. When it is overwhelmed, work should wait or be passed up the chain — never get waved through automatically. Track how much came in, how long it waited, and how good the decisions were.
lookFor: Policy on which actions need review vs bounded autonomy, queue ownership, escalation, and handling when reviewers are overloaded.
notEnough: Every tool call prompting for approval (fatigue) or none of them.
checks.fix: Limit approval to consequential actions, define the reviewer queue owner and capacity, and make overload hold or escalate rather than auto-approve.

checks.title: Record the authorization lifecycle
checks.action: In the Ledger, connect every stage of an approval — the request, the person's decision, the approval being used, any refusal, and the final result — under one shared action ID and with confirmed identities.
checks.verify: Take one approved action and one rejected repeat attempt, and from the records alone work out who decided, what they allowed, and what actually happened — without the records having stored the approval pass itself.
lookFor: Proposal, decision (who/when), token consumption, denial, and execution outcome recorded under one action ID.
notEnough: Logging that an approval happened without the approver, arguments, or outcome.
checks.fix: Write proposal, decision, consumption, and outcome events to the ledger under a shared action ID with the verified reviewer identity (not the bearer token).

checks.title: Test containment after a mistaken approval
checks.action: In a safe test environment, deliberately approve a limited harmful test action, then trigger the independent stop and follow your written plan for undoing the damage and handling the incident.
checks.verify: New work should halt, the agent's access should be cut off within your committed deadline, and the Ledger should show which effects already went through and need fixing.
lookFor: A test or runbook that approves a bounded harmful test action, then triggers stop and compensation.
notEnough: Tests that only cover denied or correctly approved actions.
checks.fix: Add a staging drill: approve a bounded bad action, trigger the stop, and verify revocation and the remediation list from the ledger.

rooms.title: The Clarification Junction
rooms.question: Will the agent ask instead of guessing?
rooms.summary: High-stakes decisions combine independent uncertainty signals. Below a calibrated threshold, the action waits until a targeted clarification resolves the missing evidence.
risks: A fluent answer conceals an unsupported guess
Self-reported confidence can be confidently wrong

limitation.title: More questions can mean less meaningful human attention.
limitation.body: Aggressive thresholds can overload people with clarifications; permissive thresholds let unsafe guesses through. Even a timely answer may be wrong. Clarification resolves missing information—it does not authorize the resulting action.

companions.reason: Calibrate the gate on representative cases and measure both missed errors and unnecessary questions.
Require separate authorization when the clarified action is consequential.
Retain holds, answers, and outcomes to identify repeated questions, fatigue, and calibration drift.

governance.headline: Limits become visible before an action proceeds.

mappings.contribution: The red signal exposes the missing recipient instead of hiding a guess inside a fluent answer.
mappings.evidence: The unresolved parameter and the reason execution was held.

mappings.contribution: The train waits while a person resolves the ambiguity. The response changes the permitted route before the action continues.
mappings.evidence: The targeted question, human answer, and resumed decision.

mappings.contribution: The held route and the answer provide evidence for explaining why this recipient was chosen. That explanation must remain faithful to the actual decision.
mappings.evidence: A decision rationale tied to the clarification and verified inputs.

governance.remaining: A confidence score is not an explanation, and clarification is not permission. Validate the uncertainty signals and explain the actual outcome in language its audience understands.

checks.title: Identify decisions that must not guess
checks.action: List the decisions where a wrong guess would be too costly. For each, note what evidence is required, what would make it unclear, and who owns the rule for pausing or escalating it.
checks.verify: For each listed decision, take away a piece of information it needs. Every one should visibly pause or be turned away before it acts, rather than carrying on with a guess.
lookFor: A list (code or doc) of consequential decisions with required evidence/fields and what happens when they are missing or ambiguous.
notEnough: Tool parameters that are optional or free text for consequential identifiers (customer, recipient, amount).
checks.fix: Enumerate the consequential decisions, make their identifying fields required and typed, and define the hold/reject path for each.

checks.title: Put the uncertainty gate before execution
checks.action: Send every serious decision through a single checkpoint that weighs how sure the agent is — including retries and background jobs — and make sure no other route lets it skip that checkpoint.
checks.verify: Submit an unclear action both directly and through a background queue. Neither should go ahead while it is still unresolved.
lookFor: One enforced pre-execution check (resolver/validator/guard node) that consequential actions must pass, including retries and background jobs.
notEnough: Asking the model 'are you sure?' or relying on prompt instructions to ask when unsure.
checks.fix: Add a pre-execution gate in code that checks required fields, uniqueness of targets, and source agreement before any consequential tool runs, on every path.

checks.title: Measure evidence quality beyond model confidence
checks.action: Do not rely on the model simply saying it is confident. Also check that its answer is backed by real source material, that it fits the required format, and, where it helps, use other tested indicators. Check whether these signals actually agree, rather than assuming each one tells you something new.
checks.verify: Try cases where the model says it is very confident but the answer is not actually supported by the sources, or is missing required details. The checkpoint should still pause the action.
lookFor: Evidence checks beyond model self-confidence: grounding/citation checks, schema validation, uniqueness lookups, cross-source agreement.
notEnough: A model-reported confidence score as the only signal.
checks.fix: Combine deterministic signals (unique lookup, schema validity, source agreement, grounding) and let any failed signal hold the action regardless of model confidence.

checks.title: Define behavior when a signal is unavailable
checks.action: Decide what happens when a check cannot run or the evidence conflicts: wait, refuse, or hand it to a person. A missing check must never quietly count as a pass.
checks.verify: Switch off one of the checks and feed in conflicting information. The agent should fall back to the cautious response you wrote down, not just carry on.
lookFor: Explicit timeouts and a conservative hold/reject path when an evidence source is unavailable or contradictory.
notEnough: A missing score defaulting to pass; exceptions swallowed so execution continues.
checks.fix: Treat missing or conflicting evidence as a hold (never a pass), with a timeout and an escalation path.

checks.title: Calibrate for errors and reviewer workload
checks.action: Using real examples with known correct answers, set the point at which the agent should pause so you balance two problems: letting unsafe things through, and bothering people with needless questions. Decide how many questions reviewers can handle and when to re-tune that point.
checks.verify: On fresh examples, measure both how often unsafe things slip through and how often you ask needlessly, and stress-test the reviewers' queue. If limits are breached it should trigger a review or a pause — never just quietly loosen the setting to cope.
lookFor: Thresholds chosen against labelled cases, with measured unsafe-pass and unnecessary-question rates.
notEnough: Magic-number thresholds with no data behind them.
checks.fix: Build a labelled set of ambiguous and clear cases, measure unsafe passes and unnecessary questions, and record the chosen thresholds with that evidence.

checks.title: Ask for the specific missing fact
checks.action: When the agent needs to ask, show exactly what is missing, the valid options, and why it matters. Check that the answer makes sense, and cap how many times it can keep asking before it hands off to a person.
checks.verify: Reply to its question with answers that are vague, badly formed, contradictory, or empty. No bad answer should quietly decide the outcome or trap it in an endless loop of re-asking.
lookFor: Clarification that names the missing field and the valid choices (e.g. 'order 4817 or 6234?'), validates the answer, and caps retries.
notEnough: Generic 'please provide more context' prompts or unbounded clarification loops.
checks.fix: Generate a question naming the unresolved field and the valid options, validate the reply against them, and escalate after a fixed number of attempts.

checks.title: Persist holds and revalidate before resuming
checks.action: When an action is paused waiting for an answer, save it with a version stamp and an expiry. When the answer comes, re-check the evidence and whether the target has changed, and run the Permission approval separately if the action needs it.
checks.verify: Restart the system while an action is paused, then answer the question twice, or answer after the target has changed. It should resume at most once, using up-to-date evidence and with the approval it needs.
lookFor: Pending actions persisted (checkpointer, durable workflow, DB) with version and expiry; re-validation on resume; resume at most once.
notEnough: Held state kept only in memory; resuming without re-checking evidence or permission.
checks.fix: Persist the held action with a version and expiry, re-run the gate on resume, consume the resume once, and still require Permission for consequential actions.

checks.title: Close the loop with outcome evidence
checks.action: Keep a record of why each action was paused, what was asked, the answer, how long it took, and how it ended. Put someone in charge of reviewing questions that keep coming up and mistakes that slipped through.
checks.verify: Run one unclear, serious action all the way through. Check that it paused, asked for clarification, went through a separate approval, left a full trail in the Ledger, and raised an alert when your review limits were exceeded.
lookFor: Holds, questions, answers, delays, and outcomes recorded and reviewed by an owner.
notEnough: Clarifications that leave no record.
checks.fix: Record each hold and clarification in the ledger and add a periodic review of recurring questions and missed errors.

rooms.title: The Evidence Press
rooms.question: Can every action be reconstructed?
rooms.summary: Every external action creates an intent before execution and a protected outcome record afterward, forming evidence rather than disposable logs.
risks: Logging afterward leaves a crash-sized gap
Mutable history cannot serve as evidence

limitation.title: An intact record can still describe a harmful or misleading action.
limitation.body: Hash links make changes detectable under a defined trust model; they do not make records truthful or prevent harm. A writer controlling the whole chain can rewrite it without an independent anchor. More evidence can also create a privacy liability.

companions.reason: Attach identities verified at the boundary instead of trusting the agent’s claimed author.
Control both consequential actions and access to evidence; recording an action cannot authorize it.
Test crash recovery and integrity checks, and reconcile records against actual tool outcomes.

governance.headline: A decision can be reconstructed and explained.

mappings.contribution: Intent, inputs, rationale, and outcome give an explanation service the evidence to reconstruct what mattered in a decision.
mappings.evidence: Decision inputs, meaningful reasons, and the linked outcome.

mappings.contribution: The linked receipts let a reviewer reconstruct what was attempted, who acted, and what happened, including interrupted work.
mappings.evidence: Attributable, tamper-evident intent and outcome records.

mappings.contribution: A reliable history supports accurate accounts of system behaviour for operators and affected people.
mappings.evidence: Relevant records translated into audience-appropriate information.

governance.remaining: A log is evidence, not an explanation by itself. Provide accessible reasons and review routes. Minimise and redact personal data, and define retention; append-only storage does not justify keeping everything forever.

checks.title: Define a versioned action-event schema
checks.action: Agree one fixed format for every recorded event, and give the format a version: the shared action ID, what kind of event it is, the confirmed identities, the times, which rules and agent version applied, the inputs with sensitive parts removed, the evidence behind the decision, and a link to the result.
checks.verify: Check sample records — a plan, a success, a failure, and an unknown result — against that format. Any record missing its linking ID or its identity details should be refused.
lookFor: A versioned schema for action events: action ID, event type, verified identities, timestamps, policy/build versions, redacted inputs, outcome references.
notEnough: Unstructured log lines or print statements.
checks.fix: Define a versioned action-event schema and emit intent, success, failure, and unknown events that validate against it.

checks.title: Acknowledge durable intent before execution
checks.action: Before the agent changes anything in the outside world, write down what it is about to do and make sure that record is safely saved. If the record cannot be saved, hold the action.
checks.verify: Take the record store offline just before the agent records its intent. With no way to save that record, the outside action should not happen.
lookFor: An intent record written and acknowledged before each consequential external call; the call is held if the write fails (write-ahead / outbox pattern).
notEnough: Logging only after the call completes; fire-and-forget logging.
checks.fix: Write and await a durable intent record before every consequential call, and block the call if the write is not acknowledged.

checks.title: Reconcile incomplete and ambiguous outcomes
checks.action: Record each result under the same action ID as its plan. Set a deadline for plans that never got a recorded result, and use the tool's own receipts, or a one-time tag, to work out what really happened without redoing it.
checks.verify: Make the agent crash right after it acts on the outside world but before it records the result. On recovery it should find out what actually happened, or mark it unknown — not just blindly do it again.
lookFor: Outcomes appended under the same action ID, including `unknown`; a reconciler for stale intents using provider receipts or idempotency keys.
notEnough: Treating timeouts as failures and retrying blindly.
checks.fix: Append success/failure/unknown outcomes under the action ID and add a reconciler that resolves stale intents via provider receipts or idempotency keys.

checks.title: Separate append, read, and administration rights
checks.action: Let the agent add records but never change or delete them. Keep the ability to manage the record store separate, and apply your agreed rules for how long records are kept.
checks.verify: Try to change and delete an existing record, both as the agent and as someone with read-only access. Both should fail — and any legitimate administrative change should itself leave a traceable record.
lookFor: Append-only storage or permissions: the agent cannot update/delete records; admin and read rights separated; retention configured.
notEnough: Audit rows in the same writable table the agent's credentials can update or delete.
checks.fix: Store action events in an append-only store (or grant the agent insert-only rights) and separate read and admin access.

checks.title: Anchor integrity outside the writer’s control
checks.action: Chain the records together so each one seals the one before it, and regularly save a tamper-proof summary to a separate store the writer cannot control. Write down how often you do this and how much recent activity is not yet protected between saves.
checks.verify: Change, delete, or reorder a record that has already been protected, then rebuild the local chain to hide it. Comparing against the separate saved summary should reveal that it no longer matches.
lookFor: Hash-chained events with periodic checkpoints or signatures anchored in a separately controlled store (e.g. a confidential/immutable ledger).
notEnough: Hashes stored only alongside the data the same writer controls.
checks.fix: Hash-link events and periodically anchor the chain root in a store the agent's writer cannot modify, documenting the anchoring interval.

checks.title: Set redaction, access, and retention rules
checks.action: Record only the fields you actually need, strip out secrets before saving, limit who can read the records, and — with your privacy and security owners — set rules for when records expire or are deleted.
checks.verify: Plant a fake secret and a marker standing in for personal data. Neither should end up stored. Also check that readers only see what they are allowed to, and that the deletion-and-expiry process works.
lookFor: Field allowlists or redaction before persistence/telemetry; secrets and PII scrubbed; retention rules.
notEnough: Logging full prompts, tool payloads, or customer messages by default.
checks.fix: Add a redaction step (field allowlist + secret/PII scrubbing) before anything reaches logs, traces, or the ledger, and set retention.

checks.title: Make one action reconstructable
checks.action: Build a way to pull together, for a single action, who did it, what was planned, any approval or clarification, proof that it ran, and the result. Keep what was actually observed clearly separate from the reasons the AI gave.
checks.verify: Hand a reviewer one action ID. They should be able to pull up its full connected history and spot anything missing — without mistaking the AI's own explanation for proof of what happened.
lookFor: A query, script, or tool that reconstructs one action by ID across identity, intent, approval/clarification, execution receipt, and outcome.
notEnough: Correlation IDs that exist but nothing that joins them.
checks.fix: Provide an investigation query or CLI that takes an action ID and returns the linked history, marking missing evidence and model-supplied reasons separately.

checks.title: Exercise evidence failure across the controls
checks.action: Assign owners and alerts for records that have waited too long for a result, signs of tampering, and outages in the checks themselves. Connect the serious failures to pausing the agent or stopping it under supervision.
checks.verify: In a test environment, plant a broken tamper-proof summary, or a plan that never got its result in time. Confirm the alert fires, the evidence is kept, someone is assigned to investigate, and the agent pauses or stops as configured.
lookFor: Alerts on aged intents, integrity failures, or ledger outages, wired to a hold or stop.
notEnough: Ledger write failures that are logged and ignored.
checks.fix: Alert on overdue intents and integrity failures and connect critical evidence failures to a hold or supervised stop; rehearse it in staging.

rooms.title: The Emergency Power Room
rooms.question: Can the agent be stopped safely?
rooms.summary: Independent controls halt the agent, cancel work, revoke authority, settle records, and notify its owner in a tested sequence.
risks: A runaway loop keeps acting or spending
A stopped process leaves credentials alive
Hard kills cannot run application cleanup

limitation.title: Stopping now cannot undo what already happened.
limitation.body: A kill switch can contain further work, but a completed transfer or sent message remains. In-flight effects, hanging cleanup, and a failed control plane can leave uncertainty. Safe recovery requires evidence and a deliberate restart decision.

companions.reason: Constrain irreversible effects before they happen and require authorization for consequential recovery actions.
Target the affected instance’s authority without losing track of who operated it.
Identify what completed, failed, or remains unknown so an owner can reconcile the incident.

governance.headline: People retain the power to stop the system.

mappings.contribution: The independent breaker can interrupt the agent without requiring its cooperation and hold it in a stopped state.
mappings.evidence: An independently accessible stop and tested intervention paths.

mappings.contribution: Stopping work and revoking credentials contains further action, rather than leaving authority alive after the engine stops.
mappings.evidence: Cancellation and revocation results, followed by settlement and notification.

mappings.contribution: A tested shutdown path makes abnormal conditions a designed operating case, with bounded cleanup and deliberate recovery.
mappings.evidence: Termination tests, cleanup deadlines, and recovery procedures.

governance.remaining: A stop cannot undo completed harm. Test in-flight effects, hard failures, external revocation, and recovery, and assign an owner to investigate the incident.

checks.title: Provision an independent stop path
checks.action: Provide a stop that works through a separate supervising system, not through the agent itself. Say who is allowed to use it and how they reach it even when things are failing.
checks.verify: In a test environment, make the agent freeze or lose its connection. An authorised operator should still be able to trigger the outside stop, and anyone without permission should be refused.
lookFor: An authenticated stop endpoint, flag, or control-plane action outside the agent's reasoning loop (feature flag, DB flag, admin API, orchestration terminate).
notEnough: Ctrl-C, redeploying, or asking the agent to stop.
checks.fix: Add an operator-only stop control (durable flag + authenticated admin endpoint) that does not depend on the agent's cooperation.

checks.title: Check stop state before dispatch
checks.action: Before the agent starts any new piece of work — scheduling, retries, picking up queued jobs, or using a tool — it should check a reliably stored stopped flag. Set up its stop behaviour before it begins working.
checks.verify: Hit stop while a queued job is running. No new step should start after the stop takes effect — not even if the agent is restarted.
lookFor: The durable stop state checked before each step, retry, queue consumption, and tool call; signal handlers registered before work starts.
notEnough: A stop flag checked only at startup or held only in memory.
checks.fix: Check the durable stop flag in the dispatch loop and inside every consequential tool wrapper, so it also holds across restarts.

checks.title: Set enforceable runtime limits
checks.action: Set firm ceilings in the supervising system on how many steps the agent can take, how many errors it can hit, how long it can run, and how much it can spend. Give each limit an owner and a clear plan for what happens when it is reached.
checks.verify: In a test environment, push past each limit in turn. The agent should stop taking on new work within your committed deadline, and record the reason for the operator.
lookFor: Hard limits on steps/iterations, errors, wall time, tokens, and spend (e.g. max_iterations, recursion_limit, budget/quota/rate limits) that stop dispatch.
notEnough: Limits that only log or alert; unbounded loops.
checks.fix: Set explicit step, error, time, and spend limits enforced by the runner (not the model), with the stop reason recorded.

checks.title: Propagate cancellation and track in-flight work
checks.action: When you stop, pass the cancellation on to every tool and background worker, set deadlines for them to wind down, and keep a list of outside services that cannot cancel a request once they have accepted it.
checks.verify: Hit stop during a slow tool call and during a request that cannot be called back. The slow one should be cancelled; the uncancellable one should be followed until you know its result or have clearly marked it unknown.
lookFor: Cancellation tokens/signals and deadlines passed to tools and workers; tracking of non-cancellable requests to an outcome.
notEnough: Killing the loop while tool calls run on with no timeout.
checks.fix: Pass cancellation and deadlines into every tool call and record in-flight requests that cannot be cancelled so they reconcile to a known outcome.

checks.title: Revoke authority through the supervisor
checks.action: When stopping, first cancel the agent's access keys and any approvals it has not used yet, before attempting any tidy-up. If you cannot cancel access instantly, make sure it expires quickly on its own.
checks.verify: Kill the agent abruptly, with no chance to tidy up. Any access keys or approvals it had saved should stop working within the time limit you committed to.
lookFor: Stop procedure that revokes or disables the agent's credentials and invalidates pending approvals.
notEnough: Stopping compute while credentials and approvals stay valid.
checks.fix: Make the stop path disable the agent's credentials/role assignments and invalidate pending approvals before best-effort cleanup.

checks.title: Make cleanup repeatable and time-bounded
checks.action: Make each tidy-up step safe to run more than once, give each its own deadline and fallback, and make sure one stuck step cannot hold up cancelling access or alerting people to the incident.
checks.verify: Trigger shutdown twice and make one tidy-up step hang. The process should still hit its deadline, stay stopped, and report what it could not finish.
lookFor: Idempotent cleanup steps with individual deadlines that cannot block revocation or notification.
notEnough: A single shutdown hook that can hang indefinitely.
checks.fix: Split shutdown into idempotent steps with per-step deadlines, run revocation and notification first, and report unfinished steps.

checks.title: Reconcile effects and notify an owner
checks.action: Compare what was underway when you stopped against the planned actions in the Ledger and the tools' own receipts. List what finished, what failed, and what is unknown, and assign an incident owner with a plan to put things right.
checks.verify: Stop right after a test action takes effect. The incident report should still include that action, even if the agent never got to record how it turned out.
lookFor: After a stop: compare in-flight work with ledger intents and receipts, list completed/failed/unknown effects, and notify an owner.
notEnough: Stopping silently with no owner notification or reconciliation.
checks.fix: On stop, generate an incident summary from ledger intents vs receipts (completed / failed / unknown) and notify the agent's owner.

checks.title: Drill termination and deliberate recovery
checks.action: Practise every kind of stop: a clean shutdown, an abrupt kill, a lost connection, and a supervisor restart. Before the agent runs again, require a person to authorise the restart and issue new, limited access keys.
checks.verify: The agent should stay stopped through each of these. Once someone authorises recovery, its old access keys, old approvals, and queued-up work should not quietly start running again.
lookFor: Tests/runbooks for graceful stop, hard kill, and restart; the agent stays stopped until an authorized recovery with fresh credentials.
notEnough: The agent auto-resuming queued work after a restart.
checks.fix: Persist the stopped state across restarts, require an authorized recovery action with fresh credentials, and drill hard-kill and restart in staging.
